title: Acceleration-induced spectral blind spots in stimulated atomic transitions
abstract: Stimulated transitions are among the most fundamental processes in light-matter interaction, underlying resonant absorption and emission in atomic systems. Here we show that uniform acceleration can convert this familiar response into a frequency-selective absence of response. Specifically, when an incident photon has a nonzero momentum component transverse to the acceleration, the stimulated transition probability vanishes at a discrete set of frequencies fixed by the acceleration, the atomic transition frequency, and the photon propagation angle. At these spectral blind spots, both ordinary stimulated absorption and acceleration-induced excitation are simultaneously suppressed, rendering the atom effectively unresponsive to the incident radiation. The effect arises from the nontrivial response of accelerated atoms to quantum vacuum fluctuations and provides a distinctive signature of the Unruh effect through the absence, rather than the enhancement, of stimulated transitions. We further provide an order-of-magnitude estimate showing that an electron-based implementation with spin splitting in combined electric and magnetic fields could access the required parameter regime. These results reveal an unexplored form of acceleration-modified light-matter interaction and identify spectral blind spots as a new manifestation of the Unruh effect.
summary: The paper theoretically demonstrates that uniform acceleration can induce spectral blind spots in atomic transitions by modifying light-matter coupling. These blind spots manifest as frequencies where both normal stimulated absorption and Unruh excitation are simultaneously suppressed, providing a unique signature of the Unruh effect through signal absence.
main_problem: The study investigates how uniform acceleration fundamentally alters the stimulated light-matter interaction response of an atom, potentially leading to frequency-selective spectral blind spots.
main_result: Spectral blind spots occur at discrete frequencies where both ordinary stimulated absorption and acceleration-induced Unruh excitation simultaneously vanish for photons with transverse momentum.
method: The analysis uses quantum electrodynamics formalism applied to a two-level atom coupled to a massless scalar field along an accelerated trajectory, involving Bessel functions.
model_or_system:
The system is a uniformly accelerated two-level atom interacting weakly with the quantized electromagnetic vacuum field. The calculations distinguish between oblique ($k_\perp 
eq 0$) and collinear ($k_\perp = 0$) driving fields.
key_observables: Stimulated transition probability, spectral blind spots (frequencies where absorption and excitation vanish).
important_parameters: Proper acceleration ($a$), atomic transition frequency ($\omega_0$), transverse photon momentum component ($k_\perp$).
main_assumptions: Weak coupling ($\lambda$) is assumed, and the analysis focuses on uniform acceleration trajectories in natural units.
figures_summary: Figure 1 plots a function involving modified Bessel functions of the second kind, $K_2 i\omega_0/a(k_\perp/a)$, which governs both transition probabilities for transversely propagating photons.
paper_structure: The paper develops the theory by calculating transition amplitudes using field mode expansions along an accelerated path. It then derives and analyzes the resulting stimulated absorption and Unruh excitation probabilities, contrasting the results for oblique versus collinear driving fields to pinpoint the spectral suppression mechanism.
why_interesting: This work provides a novel signature of the Unruh effect—a frequency-dependent *absence* of response rather than an expected enhancement—which is highly relevant for quantum optics and open system dynamics in non-inertial frames.
